title: Converting a Furnace To A Heat Pump!
summary: A Georgia HVAC contractor replaces a failing furnace and AC with a heat pump without heat strips, saying it cost $3,000 less than a furnace-and-AC replacement and will cut the tenants' bills.

assertions.quote: it would have cost him $3,000 more than the system that I just installed

verdicts.note: When both systems are due, a heat pump's extra cost over a new AC is small, so payback is far shorter than when replacing working equipment.
Homes without existing AC are doubly challenged: higher bills from new cooling and a higher incremental cost because there is no AC replacement to offset.

RMI finds heat pump retrofits of gas homes generally cost more, with the notable exception of a customer replacing both furnace and AC, whom one heat pump serves (true in Houston, Chicago and Oakland but not Providence).
LBNL: the heat pump's cost premium over gas equipment disappears once cooling must also be added (like-for-like heating plus cooling), which is the case when the air conditioner also needs replacing.
Retrofit paybacks typically exceed 10 years unless equipment needs replacing; at heating or cooling system failure the payback drops to 5-6 years.
Incremental cost falls to $4,270 at AC failure and $370 when furnace and AC both fail (payback 0.6-1.1 years), versus 14.5-28.8 years with no failure.
Doubling as cooling is one reason heat pumps beat gas plus AC on lifetime cost, but the model always compares full replacements and does not test the case where only the furnace is due.

assertions.quote: that bill is going to be much smaller for them
They can replace a gas furnace down here and make the house safer.

verdicts.note: In mild southern climates a properly sized heat pump covers the design heating load without resistance backup.
Backup heating may not be needed in moderate climates such as southwestern British Columbia; the model includes it anyway to be conservative.
